I'm a network engineer and I currently hold a CCNP R&S and CCNA Security.

If you want to be a network engineer, I would 100% recommend getting some Cisco certs. They have consistently proven to have the best ROI of any certs (or even degrees) I have ever gotten. In fact I currently work for a Cisco Partner who is sponsoring my CCIE.

The certs you get should really just be an extension of what you want to get into. The CCNA R&S is the cornerstone of the whole Cisco cert program. You will need to get that before you can branch off, so start there. You can either take it as one big test, or take it as two tests. If you take it as two, the first test will get you a CCENT and the second the CCNA. Once you have that you should have an idea if you want to dive down the rabbit hole and continue up the core networking track, or spread out and know about more stuff at the same level.

How does the CCNA compare with the CCNP?

The CCNA R&S is fairly basic. It's what you would want to know if your network is fairly small and pretty typical.

The CCNP R&S is much more comprehensive. It covers most of what you would want to know to build and troubleshoot large and complex networks.

The CCIE R&S gets into a lot of indepth underlying topics and special use cases. It's pretty heavy on QoS, MPLS, and BGP. Which most engineers don't really need to know about.

What certs do you have already? Its better to get a smaller number of respected certs that cover a wide variety of topics than it is to get a bunch of mid tier certs that cover the same thing. And don't even think you can just get a dozen certs with no respect behind them and have that be equal to some of the more prestigious (and stupidly expensive) ones. That being said, Cisco is well respected, and certainly their certs are in demand FOR PLACES USING CISCO HARDWARE. Cisco, being an industry juggernaut, can get away with some of their products being radically different than the competition. This makes their certs way more valuable to some, but worthless to those that don't use a ton of Cisco hardware. If you are looking at networking certs, start with the gold standard- CompTia Net+, THEN grab a CCNA. If you have net+ and want to up your networking certification game, then, yeah, the CCNA is the best family of certs to get (unless you work in an environment dealing solely with windows devices, in which case MCSE might be worth a look). I would say that security is more in demand than wireless at the moment, at least for hiring managers, and people who aren't themselves doing IT work, but that, in relevant positions, the wireless concentration will likely score more brownie points with people who actually know their stuff in networking.

Like I said in another post: I have the Net+ and Sec+. I'm probably best at the security, but I'm interested in the wireless. Right now, I'm just trying to canvas what people think of the certs and their structure.

If you have Net+ Security+, then I would err on the side of adding wireless to showcase a more diverse skillset (since Net+ is rather light on wireless iirc, but then again, I also haven't looked too closely at it since the most recent rewrite. I picked mine up before they had to renew, my version of the exam in 2009 still had questions on token ring, and the objectives defined wireless networking as a niche technology primarily useful in military applications, but not something the average consumer or business would be interested in), doubly so, since you already have sec+ (unless you are SPECIFICALLY looking for a job as a security expert, in which case you really should look at other certs, like CEH), if you decide to go with a CCNA+ Concentration.Of course, since the name of the game in the job market is diverse skills with the resume to back it up, you might want to pick up A+ or another general cert before getting another networking related one, especially a networking one that is more specialized than what you already hold(though only having credentials from 1 company doesn't look great, having them all from a vendor neutral entity like comptia is the least offensive version of this sin). If you already have credentials backing up your general computing knowledge and experience, then I would say branch out a bit. Want to be a systems administrator who lives in the terminal? Get yourself a server or linux related cert. Perhaps even something that digs deep into virtualization, like a vmware cert (though, again, unless you have a job already, be wary of vendor specific certifications, as they quickly loose value if you apply to places that don't use them, with cisco certs being about as close to an exception as you can find. Microsoft is also safe if they have certs relevant to your desired position, since everywhere uses windows, if only for the non IT employees). Or, if an amazon web services cert will work wonders, depending on what kind of company you want to work for. Want to move to management some day? Get a project management certification like a PMP. Want to go into security and stay there (seems about right from what you have listed)? Don't waste your time getting a mid level cisco cert with a security concentration tacked on. You already have security+. Anything with security as an afterthought to a cert of similar rigor to a security dedicated degree just isn't going to be as useful in a security setting. You might learn a lot about networking, which is useful to find holes, but the applications to security will be relatively minimal compared to security+, instead, look at other programs dedicated to cybersecurity (again, make sure you have a good baseline like an A+ first, though, otherwise you will look terribly 1 dimensional in your technical knowledge and expertise) like the certified ethical hacker. Want to work desktop support (don't know why you would, but hey, everyone has a taste), or need something to appeal to a hiring manager who doesn't know what the hell they are doing when hiring IT talent, and doesn't communicate well with what the CIO or IT head wants, get a microsoft cert. Alternatively, if you feel you look like you have a good, diverse skillset to potential employers, but perhaps look a little light on experience, see what you can do to show that you can apply your knowledge; participate in code jams or other competitions, and do your best to finish in a position that you can flaunt. Contribute to a linux distro or some other open source project. If you are dealing with people who are themselves IT people, and you can point to changes YOU made to a project that made it better, great.

Of course, if you have a job, this all changes. Ask you employer what THEY want out of YOU. If you let them pick, they will likely pay for it, and maybe even give you a little bump in your envelope for making yourself more useful to them.

If you have no certs, then your best bet is to get A+, Network+ and Security+ first, as all will do you well for getting other certs.
